Who's up for a thought experiment? So, I was thinking about this several months ago and it came to mind just tonight, so I thought I'd get a few more minds in on this.

Imagine the following: You live in a future where your brain can be copied at 1:1 accuracy, and brain transplants are possible, routine, and safe. This new brain is exactly the same as your old brain, flaws and all. Now, let's say you have the need for a new brain. So, they simply remove your old brain, and replace it with a new one (which is exactly the same as your old brain at the moment it was extracted).

The question: Would you wake up following the operation? It's obvious that your body would function, and it would be your body, but would it be you waking up following the operation? Would you experience the world as yourself, or would you die with your brain cells as a perfect copy of you (soon to diverge and become a different version of you with the passage of time) begins to walk the earth?

Question 2: If you woke up following the procedure, does this mean that personhood, or the self is held somewhere other than the brain? If not, how is it that the original self has survived beyond the death of the original brain? If the original you did not wake up after the operation, does this mean that there isn't a self to begin with, but we only have an illusion of a self generated by how one individual brain responds to new information and new contexts we find ourselves in?

Question 1: I believe that a carbon copy of my consciousness would wake up in my body, and it would feel like nothing had changed. The consciousness I currently am would just be gone. Question 2: I think that consciousness is an emergent property of any sufficiently advanced network. I don't think it's an illusion, but it is possible that it doesn't exist depending on your personal definition of consciousness. If I woke up though I wouldn't know it was still the same consciousness. It could have just as easily been that the original me had died, and since the new me is a carbon copy of old me, down to the memories I wouldn't be able to tell that I was a new me. New me wouldn't be able to tell if it was new me or old me either.

If we think of consciousness like a neurological version of computer state, this question becomes more concrete.

Let's call the person "P". Imagine 3 states; state "A" is the state that has logs for person "P" up until 10 minutes before the surgery/crash date, state "B" is the state that has logs for person "P" up until the surgery/crash date, and state "C" is the state that has all of the logs for person "P" up until the present. We have no problem saying that state "A" is just an earlier version of state "B", and that they both represent "P" at different points in time (ie, you consider the self you remember 10 minutes ago to be the same as the self you are now, even though they're in different locations and slightly different bodies, simply because they're connected via your memory). I'd say the same thing applies to state "C". The only difference with state "C" is that the location is very different, and there might be a gap that might weird out your sense of self because of the lack of continuity (though that already happens when you go under general anesthesia). But the old logs are still the same: if it were a computer and you were swapping out a bad hard drive and copied everything exactly as it was, you'd view your system as the same system.

This helps answer the second question; when you wake up, you are a later version of state "B", so the previous argument still applies (you're still "you"). You just aren't the later version of state "B" that's dead; if you copied your state and put it in another body before you died, there would then be two different people in existence, as you would no longer have the same inputs, and therefore would have different memories immediately following the point of divergence. The weird thing is that they would share the same earlier version of you, and would both consider themselves to own that earlier person. But that earlier person doesn't exist anymore, just as the person you were 10 minutes ago doesn't exist. That's what makes it confusing; we don't have a word for a "past self that two different people share" other than "self". We always assume only one person will share our past.
